projects.subject: physics
projects.title: The Bicycle That Would Not Stop
projects.mission: A delivery rider finds that a bicycle takes much longer to stop when carrying a heavy box and moving faster. Investigate why the stopping distance changes and decide how the rider can stay within a safe stopping distance.

sections.title: What happens when a moving object stops?
sections.content: A moving bicycle has kinetic energy. When the brakes are applied, this energy has to be removed. It mainly changes into heat in the brake system and tyres. A bicycle with more kinetic energy needs more braking work to stop.

sections.title: What changes kinetic energy?
sections.content: Kinetic energy depends on mass and speed. KE = 1/2 mv², where m is mass in kg and v is speed in m/s. Speed is squared. If speed doubles, kinetic energy becomes four times larger when mass stays the same.

sections.title: Simple example
sections.content: For a 20 kg object moving at 5 m/s, KE = 1/2 × 20 × 5² = 250 J. If its speed becomes 10 m/s, KE = 1/2 × 20 × 10² = 1000 J.

sections.title: Braking
sections.content: With the same braking system, more kinetic energy generally means more work is needed and the stopping distance can become larger. Speed and load both matter when checking braking safety.

levels.title: The First Test

questions.prompt: A bicycle and rider have the same total mass in two tests. In the second test the speed is doubled. Which quantity changes strongly because of the speed change?
hints: Which quantity describes the energy of a moving object?
Check which variable is squared in KE = 1/2 mv².

questions.prompt: The bicycle and rider have a total mass of 50 kg and move at 4 m/s. Find the kinetic energy.
hints: Use KE = 1/2 mv².
Square the speed before multiplying.

questions.prompt: The same 50 kg bicycle and rider now move at 8 m/s. How many times is the kinetic energy compared with the 4 m/s case?
hints: Compare the speeds first.
The speed term is squared.

levels.title: The Heavy Box

questions.prompt: Two tests use the same speed of 6 m/s. Test A has a total mass of 50 kg. Test B has a total mass of 75 kg. Which test has more kinetic energy?
hints: Keep speed fixed and compare mass.
Mass is part of KE = 1/2 mv².

questions.prompt: A loaded bicycle has mass 75 kg and speed 6 m/s. Find its kinetic energy.
hints: Substitute 75 kg and 6 m/s.

questions.prompt: The rider says, 'The bicycle is safe because the speed did not change.' The load increased from 50 kg to 75 kg. Which statement is correct?
options: The load increases kinetic energy at the same speed.
hints: Ask what happens when mass increases while speed stays fixed.
Mass is part of the kinetic-energy formula.

levels.title: Safe Route Decision

questions.prompt: The bicycle brake system can safely remove at most 1600 J of kinetic energy. A 75 kg bicycle and rider are moving at 6 m/s. Is the condition within the limit?
hints: Calculate KE first.
Compare it with 1600 J.

questions.prompt: For the same 75 kg bicycle and rider, find the greatest speed that gives exactly 1600 J of kinetic energy. Give the answer to 2 decimal places.
hints: Set KE equal to the limit.
Rearrange to find v.

questions.prompt: Which route condition stays below the 1600 J braking limit?
hints: Calculate KE for each option.
The selected condition must be below 1600 J.

projects.subject: physics
projects.title: The Solar Panel That Lost Power
projects.mission: A small solar-powered charging station produces less electrical power than expected. The panel and battery are working, so the team suspects that the direction of incoming sunlight is affecting output. Investigate the effect of angle and choose a useful setup.

learningCapsule.title: Light, Surface Area and Solar Power

sections.title: Why does panel direction matter?
sections.content: A solar panel receives energy from sunlight. A larger effective area facing incoming light receives more of that light. When light arrives farther from the useful perpendicular direction, less light is received effectively.

sections.title: Simple model
sections.content: For a flat surface receiving light at an angle θ from the perpendicular, the simple model is P = Pmax cos θ. θ is measured from the perpendicular. At θ = 0°, power is maximum.

sections.title: Example
sections.content: If Pmax = 100 W and θ = 60°, then P = 100 × cos 60° = 50 W.

sections.title: Important
sections.content: Do not confuse the angle of the panel with θ unless the situation defines them as the same. Real output can also depend on clouds, temperature, shading, dust and electrical losses.

levels.title: Find the Lost Power

questions.prompt: A panel gives maximum output when sunlight travels along the panel's perpendicular direction. What is θ?
hints: The perpendicular is the reference direction.
No angle away from the perpendicular means 0°.

questions.prompt: A panel can produce 120 W at θ = 0°. If θ = 60°, use P = Pmax cos θ to find the power.
hints: Multiply maximum power by 0.5.

questions.prompt: Which angle gives more modeled power for the same panel: θ = 20° or θ = 70°?
hints: Compare how close each angle is to 0°.
Cosine decreases from 0° toward 90°.

levels.evidenceUse: Read the mission evidence files before answering this level.
levels.simulationUse: Use the required mission simulation before answering this level.

levels.title: Test the Panel

questions.prompt: A 100 W panel gives 100 W at 0°, 87 W at 30°, and 51 W at 60°. Which measurement is closest to the simple cosine model?
hints: Calculate the model value for each angle.
Compare measured and model values.

questions.prompt: Using the same 100 W panel, estimate the modeled output at θ = 30°. Give the answer to 1 decimal place.
hints: Multiply by 100 W.

questions.prompt: The team sees lower output on a cloudy day even though the angle is unchanged. What should they conclude?
options: The simple angle model does not include every real-world factor.
hints: Look at what changed while the angle stayed the same.
A model can describe one important factor without describing everything.

levels.evidenceUse: Read the mission evidence files before answering this level.
levels.simulationUse: Use the required mission simulation before answering this level.

levels.title: Choose the Setup

questions.prompt: A 200 W panel is receiving sunlight at θ = 60°. Find the modeled power.
hints: Use P = Pmax cos θ.

questions.prompt: The station needs at least 170 W from a 200 W panel. Which angles are acceptable under the simple model?
hints: Calculate or estimate the output for each option.
The requirement is at least 170 W.

questions.prompt: Why should the team still check the panel in real sunlight after choosing an angle from the model?
options: The model ignores factors such as cloud cover and panel losses.
The panel produces power without sunlight.
hints: Think about what the model does not contain.
A simple model is not a complete real-world description.

projects.subject: economics
projects.title: The Canteen Price Problem
projects.mission: A school canteen raises the price of a popular snack. Sales fall, but the canteen is unsure whether the price increase improved total revenue. Investigate the data and help the canteen choose a price.

sections.title: Demand and quantity demanded
sections.content: Demand describes how much consumers are willing and able to buy at different prices. Quantity demanded is the amount bought at one particular price. When other conditions stay the same, a higher price usually leads to a lower quantity demanded for an ordinary good.

sections.title: Example
sections.content: If a canteen sells 100 sandwiches at ₹20, revenue is ₹2000. If the price becomes ₹25 and sales fall to 80, revenue is ₹2000. A higher price does not automatically mean higher revenue.

sections.title: Using data
sections.content: Do not look only at price or only at quantity. Compare both together when checking revenue.

levels.title: Read the Sales Data

questions.prompt: The canteen records ₹20 → 100 sandwiches, ₹25 → 80 sandwiches, ₹30 → 60 sandwiches. What pattern is shown?
options: Quantity sold falls as price rises.
Quantity sold rises as price rises.
Price and quantity do not change.
hints: Read price and quantity together.
Look at the direction of both changes.

questions.prompt: At ₹20, the canteen sells 100 sandwiches. Find total revenue.
hints: Use Total Revenue = Price × Quantity Sold.
Multiply 20 by 100.

questions.prompt: At ₹25, the canteen sells 80 sandwiches. Find total revenue.
hints: Multiply the new price by the new quantity.
Compare with the ₹20 case.

levels.evidenceUse: Read the mission evidence files before answering this level.
levels.simulationUse: Use the required mission simulation before answering this level.

levels.title: Find the Better Price

questions.prompt: Using ₹20 → 100 units, ₹25 → 80 units, ₹30 → 60 units, which prices give the highest revenue?
hints: Calculate revenue for all three prices.
Two prices can have the same revenue.

questions.prompt: The manager says, '₹30 gives more money per sandwich, so it must give more total revenue.' What is wrong?
options: Total revenue also depends on how many sandwiches are sold.
Revenue is always equal to cost.
hints: Look at the revenue formula.
Ask what happens to quantity when price rises.

questions.prompt: Suppose the price stays at ₹25 but sales increase from 80 to 100 sandwiches. What is the new revenue?
hints: The price is still ₹25.
Only quantity changes to 100.

levels.evidenceUse: Read the mission evidence files before answering this level.
levels.simulationUse: Use the required mission simulation before answering this level.

levels.title: Make the Canteen Decision

questions.prompt: Expected sales are ₹22 → 95 sandwiches, ₹25 → 86 sandwiches, ₹28 → 70 sandwiches. Find revenue at ₹22.
hints: Use price × quantity.

questions.prompt: Using the same survey, which option gives the highest expected revenue?
hints: Calculate all three revenues.
Do not choose only by highest price or highest quantity.

questions.prompt: The canteen wants the highest expected revenue from the three tested prices. Which price should it choose?
hints: Use the revenue results from the previous question.
Choose the option that meets the stated goal.

projects.subject: economics
projects.title: The Bus Fare Decision
projects.mission: A city bus service wants to change its fare. The operator wants more revenue, but the city also wants to keep enough passengers using the service. Use passenger data to compare the choices.

sections.title: Price and demand
sections.content: For many ordinary services, a higher price leads to a lower quantity demanded when other conditions stay the same. Some users may reduce trips, switch to another option or travel less.

sections.title: Trade-off
sections.content: A decision can have more than one goal. A bus operator may want high revenue, while the city may also require a minimum number of passenger trips. A good decision must satisfy the stated conditions.

sections.title: Example
sections.content: If a ₹10 fare produces 1000 trips, revenue is ₹10,000. If a ₹12 fare produces 850 trips, revenue is ₹10,200. Revenue increased, but passenger trips fell.

levels.title: Understand the Fare Data

questions.prompt: A bus operator records ₹10 → 1000 trips, ₹12 → 850 trips, ₹15 → 650 trips. What happens to passenger trips as fare rises?
options: Trips become zero at every fare.
hints: Compare the three trip counts.
Read the data as fare changes.

questions.prompt: At a fare of ₹12, there are 850 passenger trips. Find total fare revenue.
hints: Multiply fare by number of trips.

questions.prompt: Which statement is supported by the data?
options: A higher fare always gives lower revenue.
A higher fare can reduce trips while revenue may still rise.
Passenger trips are not affected by fare.
Revenue depends only on passenger trips.
hints: Calculate revenue at ₹10 and ₹12.
Trips and revenue can move differently.

levels.evidenceUse: Read the mission evidence files before answering this level.
levels.simulationUse: Use the required mission simulation before answering this level.

levels.title: Add a City Rule

questions.prompt: The city requires at least 800 passenger trips per day. Which tested fare fails this rule?
hints: Compare each trip count with 800.
Values below 800 fail.

questions.prompt: The operator can choose between ₹10 and ₹12 because both meet the minimum passenger rule. How much higher is the revenue at ₹12 than at ₹10?
hints: Calculate both revenues or use the values already found.
Subtract the ₹10 revenue from the ₹12 revenue.

questions.prompt: If the only goals are to meet at least 800 trips and maximize revenue among the tested options, which fare should be selected?
hints: Remove options that fail the city rule first.
Then compare revenue.

levels.title: A New Competitor

questions.prompt: A new shared-van service starts charging ₹8 for a similar trip. The bus operator notices fewer passengers at the same bus fare. What is the most direct economic change?
options: The bus route becomes longer automatically.
The number of buses must become zero.
hints: Ask what changed for passengers.
Look at the new service and its price.

questions.prompt: Which new evidence would be most useful before making another fare decision?
options: Passenger trips at different bus fares after the competitor entered
The number of seats in an unrelated train
hints: Choose evidence directly connected to bus demand and fare.
The competitor changed passenger choices.

questions.prompt: The city still requires at least 800 trips, but the old demand data may no longer be valid. What should the operator do before selecting a new fare?
options: Use the old data without checking.
hints: The market condition changed.
Old data may not describe the new market.
